transcript: Meeting header: 2026-11-17 15:00 PST — Duration 43m
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Ramos (TerraNova Head of ML), Priya Singh (Product Lead), Daniel O'Leary (CTO)

Summary: Weekly POC checkpoint focused on recent quality regressions identified in the pilot scoring; dug into prompt sets, scoring thresholds, and guardrail false positives. Agreed on targeted regression run and data handoff for guardrail tuning.
Topics: recent regression signals; prompt set A vs B differences; score threshold drift; guardrail false positives; Dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs for latency-sensitive routes; next steps and owners
[00:00] Jordan: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda review — maya will walk the regression findings, then we talk guardrails and infra options and finish with actions

[00:18] Maya: ok, show of hands, i ran the batch evaluation overnight on the 12k prompt corpus — overall pass rate is stable at 92%, but we have a cluster of failures concentrated in the invoicing and customs dialogs

[00:35] Alex: yeah we saw that in our dashboard, the false positive set is mostly around numeric formatting — decimals, comma separators — and some domain names that the model treats as entities and then halluc errors

[00:50] Maya: right and to be clear the regression looks correlated with a recent change: we switched the scoring function from BLEU-ish similarity to the new composite utility score last week, that bumped a couple edge cases below the acceptance threshold
[01:10] Priya: can you remind me what the composite utility score is composed of? i missed that change

[01:20] Maya: sure so it's 60% semantic match (embedding cosine), 20% format fidelity (regex/token match), 20% safety/guardrail score; the embedding weight increase made paraphrase changes more impactful
[01:35] Daniel: so if a paraphrase is semantically correct but formats numbers slightly differently it can get penalized more than before — which is what we're seeing

[01:50] Jordan: exact — two tradeoffs here: tighten format-fidelity rules or lower embedding weight. tightening might reduce recall for legitimate paraphrases; lowering embedding weight increases false acceptance of bad paraphrases. we need a targeted approach

[02:05] Maya: i ran an A/B where we disabled prefix KV cache for a subset — performance drop was negligible for the short sequences but it changed tokenization timing and slightly affected the model's output consistency, odd but consistent
[02:28] Alex: that's interesting — so runtime caching affects generation determinism? i thought kv cache just speeds things up

[02:36] Maya: yes it normally shouldn't change semantics, but with the custom kernel scheduling on our Dedicated runtime there are micro-timing differences that change the sampling trajectories for low-temp configs. not a huge delta but enough to flip a few borderline scores
[02:55] Priya: ok, operationally, what do you recommend? we have a go-live window end of month and cannot risk a regression in support flows

[03:06] Jordan: short-term: conservative — increase the acceptance window for the composite score on the affected intent groups and add a targeted post-filter that normalizes numeric formats before scoring. medium-term: we tune the scoring weights and run a dedicated regression suite across candidate kernels and Dedicated vs hosted variants
[03:30] Alex: can Redwood run the regression focused on the 12 failing prompts we flagged and share the diffs? we'd like to see the exact token-level divergence

[03:40] Maya: yes we will. i'll re-run with three variants: (1) current composite score, (2) lowered embedding weight, (3) current score but pre-normalize numbers. will dump token-level trace and upload the diffs
[04:05] Daniel: how long will that take?
[04:09] Maya: i expect the run and packaging to be done by Thursday 11/19. it's about a 2-hour run plus packaging and a short sanity pass

[04:22] Priya: good. separate question on guardrails — we're seeing a handful of false positives where system flags a benign vendor name as PII, blocking downstream actions. that's causing customer-facing failures
[04:36] Jordan: yes we observed that. guardrail tuning needs the raw examples plus redaction rules. Alex, can you share a sample set (anonymized) of the false positives?
[04:47] Alex: yes, we're preparing 50 examples with notes — we'll obfuscate company names but keep format intact. aim to share by tomorrow

[04:56] Maya: great — once we have those we can do two things: relax the blocker for those patterns and add a whitelist or context-aware exception rule. We'll also adjust the safety model threshold so it doesn't incorrectly escalate benign vendor tokens
[05:15] Jordan: about infra — there's been internal discussion about moving higher-volume routes to Dedicated to guarantee p95 latency. Daniel, where are you leaning?

[05:25] Daniel: cost is a concern but predictability is more important for customs desk flows; however we want to understand the unit cost delta. can you share pricing for a Dedicated pool with the suggested g4-32 config and autoscale?

[05:40] Jordan: yes i'll follow up with a two-line estimate. note that Dedicated reduces tail latency and gives better deterministic behavior which may reduce guardrail flapping — so there's an ops cost saving too
[05:58] Alex: one more note — some of our logs show a higher error rate when the sequence length exceeds 512 tokens, is that a known issue?

[06:10] Maya: we saw increased timeouts for long sequences on the hosted multi-tenant variant under burst; Dedicated with tuned kernel selection handles >512 sequences more robustly. we'll include a bench on the 512->1024 window
[06:28] Priya: if Dedicated is the right move, what's the migration effort and timeline?

[06:35] Jordan: for an initial route it can be staged in 2 weeks — config, smoke tests, and canary traffic. full staging across all routes depends on model variants but let's treat this as a targeted migration for customs/invoicing first

[06:52] Maya: back to scoring — we also found discrepancies due to tokenization differences between the off-the-shelf tokenizer and our internal token-merging patch. some vendor strings tokenized differently which impacted the regex match scoring
[07:07] Alex: ugh, tokenizer drift again, how do we eliminate that?
[07:12] Maya: two options: normalize tokens pre-score using the same tokenizer as the scoring step, or pin tokenizer version and record in the eval metadata. i recommend normalization for now
[07:26] Priya: is this likely to reoccur after model updates?

[07:31] Maya: yes unless we lock tokenizer/model combos or have an eval gate that checks tokenization diffs. Redwood's Optimize has a gate we can wire into CI to catch tokenization drift before rolling
[07:44] Jordan: action item — wire the pilot's repo into Redwood's eval gate so we get pre-deploy alerts. Maya will share the integration steps
[07:55] Maya: i'll send the small webhook + sample payload and example thresholds. it's pretty lightweight
[08:05] Alex: perfect. on compliance, Daniel asked earlier about audit trails and we need proof that the decisions and regressions are logged
[08:14] Daniel: yes our auditors want an end-to-end trail — model version, scoring decomposed, and guardrail triggers all stored for 180 days

[08:25] Jordan: Redwood can capture per-request metadata and store it in the private audit logs for Dedicated and Private deployments. i'll attach the SOC2 appendix and the audit retention config to the follow-up email
[08:40] Daniel: any red flags on encryption/KMS? we need customer-managed keys for some data types
[08:47] Jordan: we support KMS integrations on Private/Dedicated; i'll include the KMS design doc. hosted can do envelope encryption but not CMK control
[08:58] Priya: timeline check — we still aim for end-of-month pilot milestone. with these changes are we on track?

[09:06] Maya: yes if we run the targeted regression, apply the numeric normalization post-filter and tune two guardrail exceptions we should be able to clear the current blockers; finish by 11/24 to leave time for smoke tests
[09:20] Jordan: ok let's recap next steps

[09:24] Jordan: (1) maya runs three regression variants and posts diffs by 11/19, (2) terra nova provides 50 anonymized false-positive examples by 11/19, (3) jordan sends security + dedicated pricing by 11/18, (4) schedule dedicated latency bench for 11/23
[09:45] Alex: sounds good, thanks. small ask — can we get token-level traces in the diff? helps our debugging team
[09:52] Maya: yes we'll include token traces and sampling logs for the failing examples, but note there may be PII so we'll mask per your redaction guidance
[10:03] Daniel: thanks team, anything else?
[10:07] Priya: no, that's it from product. looking forward to the diffs
[10:11] Jordan: great we will follow up via email, i'll also drop links to the bench template and the integration guide. meeting adjourned

Notes: shared artifacts referenced — regression diff sheet (link: drive.redwood/regressions/tn-11-17), bench template (link: drive.redwood/benchmarks/g4-32-template), SOC2 appendix (link: drive.redwood/security/soc2-appendix)
End of transcript
